paper_metadata.title: The effect of casting temperature on the fatigue properties of cast nickel aluminide alloys

evidence.quote: The results of high cycle fatigue tests at 650 °C on several cast Ni3AI alloys are reported and compared with cast IN-713C.
The results of the fatigue tests are shown in Fig. 1 along with limited results generated on as-cast specimens of IN-713C in our laboratory.

In general, specimens cast 28 °C above the nominal temperature showed the best fatigue lives, and those cast at 28 °C below showed the worse lives.

attributes.location: internal, at locations where gamma prime from adjacent primary dendrites impinge

evidence.quote: Microporosity has been observed at locations where the y' from adjacent primary dendrites impinge [9]. This often results in porosity with a crack-like morphology

attributes.size: reduced relative to lower casting temperature

evidence.quote: A reduction in the volume fraction of microporosity and smaller pores are associated with faster cooling rates and this is responsible for the improved fatigue lives of IC-221M at higher casting temperatures.
In contrast, gas porosity is typically spherical in nature [9].

attributes.size: refined with increasing cooling rate (factor ~20 decrease in mean grain radius from 0.5 to 11 K/s)

evidence.quote: Sekhar et al. also found that the mean grain radius decreased by a factor of approximately 20 when the cooling rates were increased from 0.5 to 11 K s- ~.
Initiation was always associated with shrinkage porosity.
Cyclic lives of 107 cycles were observed in IC-221M at stresses of 517 MPa.
This represents a considerable improvement over the 107 cycle fatigue strength of IN-713C, estimated at 450 MPa.
IC-221M has at least a factor of 5 better fatigue life for equivalent stresses.
Comparison of the fatigue data for specimens cast at 28 °C above and below the nominal pouring temperature show a factor of 10 difference in average fatigue life.
Examination of fracture surfaces showed that crack initiation in the specimens occurred exclusively at internal defects, not at specimen surfaces.
Crack-like defects require less applied stress to initiate a flaw in comparison with the spherical gas pores because this morphology magnifies the local stress more.
In the absence of appreciable creep or environmental attack, a refined grain size should result in improved high cycle fatigue resistance [10].
